title: What is DFS (Depth First Search) — go as deep as possible first, then backtrack (use recursion or stack); like exploring one path fully before trying another.

s1_definition.profdef: Depth-first search is a graph and tree traversal that follows one path as far as it can go before backtracking to explore the next unexplored branch. It is naturally expressed with recursion, which uses the call stack, or iteratively with an explicit stack. A visited set prevents revisiting vertices in a graph. DFS runs in time proportional to vertices plus edges and is the basis for cycle detection, topological sort, and connected-component discovery.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the fraud team at the National Bank of India tracing a single suspicious chain of transfers. Starting from Rajesh's account, they follow the money to the next account, then from there to the next, going as deep down one trail as possible. Only when a trail dead-ends do they back up to the last branching point and follow a different trail. It is like exploring a maze by always walking forward until you hit a wall, then retracing your steps to the last junction and trying another corridor.
s1_definition.oneliner: DFS dives down one path completely, then backtracks to try the next, using recursion or a stack.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Depth-first search is a graph and tree traversal that follows one path as far as it can go before backtracking to explore the next unexplored branch. It is naturally expressed with recursion, which uses the call stack, or iteratively with an explicit stack. A visited set prevents revisiting vertices in a graph. DFS runs in time proportional to vertices plus edges and is the basis for cycle detection, topological sort, and connected-component discovery.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the fraud team at the National Bank of India tracing a single suspicious chain of transfers. Starting from Rajesh's account, they follow the money to the next account, then from there to the next, going as deep down one trail as possible. Only when a trail dead-ends do they back up to the last branching point and follow a different trail. It is like exploring a maze by always walking forward until you hit a wall, then retracing your steps to the last junction and trying another corridor.

**One line to remember:** DFS dives down one path completely, then backtracks to try the next, using recursion or a stack.

sections.s2_technical:
DFS commits to a path. From the current vertex it picks an unvisited neighbour and immediately goes there, repeating until it reaches a vertex with no unvisited neighbours, and only then does it backtrack to the previous vertex to try another branch.

The recursive form is the most natural. The method marks the current vertex visited, processes it, then for each neighbour recurses if that neighbour is unvisited. For example `visited.add(current); for (String n : graph.neighbours(current)) { if (!visited.contains(n)) dfs(n); }`. The recursion itself holds the backtracking information on the call stack, because when a call returns, control naturally resumes at the previous vertex. The iterative form replaces the call stack with an explicit stack: push the source, then repeatedly pop a vertex, process it if unvisited, and push its neighbours.

The visited set is critical in a graph to avoid infinite loops on cycles, though a plain tree does not need one because it has no cycles. DFS gives the three classic orders when applied to a tree as preorder, inorder, and postorder, depending on when you process the node relative to the recursive calls.

A senior-level point is what DFS is uniquely good at. It detects cycles by noticing an edge back to a vertex currently on the recursion stack. It produces a topological ordering of a dependency graph by recording vertices in reverse finish order. It finds connected components by running DFS from every unvisited vertex. Its memory use is proportional to the depth of the deepest path, which is usually far less than BFS's queue for a wide graph, but very deep recursion risks a stack overflow, so for extreme depth the explicit-stack iterative version is safer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud team wants to trace a complete chain of transfers starting from a suspect account, following each trail to its end before trying alternatives, to understand how far money can travel down any single path. Following one path deeply and then backtracking is exactly depth-first search.

Problem 2 — Crucially, the team needs to know whether the money forms a cycle, meaning it eventually returns to an account already in the current chain, because such a loop is a strong money-laundering signal. DFS detects a cycle the instant it encounters an edge leading back to a vertex that is still on the active recursion path.

In our mini-project we build a `MoneyTrailDFS` that performs a recursive depth-first traversal over a transfer graph, logging the order of the dive, and reports whether a back edge, indicating a cycle, is found. The demo builds a transfer network containing a cycle and runs DFS from Rajesh's account.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transfer graph where SAV2001 to CUR3001 to SAV4002, and SAV4002 goes to both SAV2001 (closing a cycle) and SAV5003. We trace from SAV2001.

Step 1: We call dive on SAV2001. It is new, so we mark it and log diving into SAV2001. Its only neighbour is CUR3001, so we immediately dive deeper.

Step 2: We dive into CUR3001. It is new, mark and log. Its only neighbour is SAV4002, so we dive deeper still, going as far down as possible.

Step 3: We dive into SAV4002. It is new, mark and log. Its first neighbour is SAV2001.

Step 4: We dive into SAV2001 again, but it is already visited, so dive returns immediately. This is the backtrack caused by an already-seen node.

Step 5: Back in SAV4002, we try its second neighbour SAV5003. We dive into it, mark and log. It has no neighbours, so we backtrack.

Step 6: Control unwinds back through SAV4002, CUR3001, and SAV2001, each backtracking after its branches are exhausted. The trace visited four accounts in deep-first order.

Step 7: The cycle detector runs separately. Diving SAV2001 to CUR3001 to SAV4002, it finds an edge back to SAV2001 which is still on the active path, so it reports a cycle, flagging a potential laundering loop.

```
[2026-10-26 20:30:02] INFO    Dive into SAV2001
[2026-10-26 20:30:02] INFO    Dive into CUR3001
[2026-10-26 20:30:02] INFO    Dive into SAV4002
[2026-10-26 20:30:02] INFO    Dive into SAV5003
[2026-10-26 20:30:02] INFO    DFS trace complete. Visited 4 accounts.
[2026-10-26 20:30:02] INFO    Cycle (laundering loop) detected? true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SAV2001 ──→ CUR3001 ──→ SAV4002 ──→ SAV5003
     ▲                        │
     └────────◄───────────────┘  (back edge → CYCLE)

  DFS dive order (go deep, then backtrack):
    SAV2001 → CUR3001 → SAV4002 → (SAV2001 visited, backtrack)
                               → SAV5003 (leaf, backtrack)
  Cycle detection: SAV4002→SAV2001 while SAV2001 is on active path → TRUE
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Depth-first search is a traversal that follows one path as far as it can go before backtracking to try the next unexplored branch. It is most naturally written with recursion, where the call stack itself remembers where to backtrack to, or iteratively with an explicit stack. In a graph I keep a visited set so that cycles do not send the search into an infinite loop, though a plain tree needs no such set because it has no cycles.

The mechanics I describe are straightforward. From the current vertex I mark it visited, process it, and then recurse into the first unvisited neighbour, going deeper immediately rather than looking at siblings. When a vertex has no unvisited neighbours left, the recursion returns and control resumes at the previous vertex, which is the backtracking step happening automatically.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used DFS in a money-trail tracer. The fraud team starts from a suspect account and follows each chain of transfers to its end before trying alternatives, which shows how far money can travel down any single path. More importantly, DFS detects a cycle the moment it finds an edge leading back to an account that is still on the current active path, and such a loop where money leaves and returns through intermediaries is a strong money-laundering signal, so this directly drives alerts.

The senior-level points I always raise are what DFS is uniquely good for and its tradeoffs. DFS underlies cycle detection, topological sorting of dependency graphs, and finding connected components. Its memory use is proportional to the depth of the deepest path, which is usually much less than breadth-first search's queue for a wide graph, but very deep recursion can overflow the call stack, so for extreme depth I switch to the iterative version with an explicit stack. Choosing DFS versus BFS comes down to whether I care about going deep and detecting structure, or about finding the shortest number of hops.
